utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in the courtroom. This is case IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, counsel. Mark Harmon, Carolyn Edgerton, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, and Milos Androvic, who are assisting myself, Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Just before we call the witness, I thought I must raise one or two housekeeping matters which the Chambers would like to hear the views of the parties about. It doesn't have to be today. If you're not ready, you can think about it and come back to us. First thing is wether or not the parties due intend going on a site visit, and if so, at what stage of the trial. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will think about that and get back to Your Honours very quickly with our views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honours, we would like to express our position with regard to this matter very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I will not ask you how soon. The next item that I wanted to talk about relates to the 98 bis stage of the case. In case Rule 98 bis will be made use of, depending on what the Defence thinks about the case at that time, and if we should move on to the Defence case, it is the Chamber's desire to shorten the break as much as possible at that stage. It is the belief of this Chamber that it shouldn't be -- it shouldn't take a whole motion to argue why a 98 bis ruling must be made. It can be just mentioned very quickly what it is that is alleged has not been proven and what counts, if any, or if the whole case must fall apart. The Chamber will then take a day or two to decide; and, quickly thereafter, if we have to go into the Defence case, move on speedily into the Defence case. It shouldn't take more than -- that whole break shouldn't take more than a week. Are there any comments that the parties would like to make on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the 98 bis motion rule and the proposals of the sides, well, perhaps I can reserve the right to express my position later on. My colleague Mr. Smith and myself will discuss the matter. The Defence agrees and we think it would be good for this to be made in oral form -- the arguments to be made in an oral form. And given the scope of the Prosecution case that we have before us, I believe that we will now need a certain period of time to prepare for these oral submissions, and I believe that the Prosecution will also have oral submissions to make. But I really believe that for the preparation of the Defence case, as it now stands, and for the preparation of Mr. Guy-Smith's case and in the light of the experience we have from previous cases, I do believe that we will need, well, a significant period of time, a significantly lengthy period of time that you referred to, Judge Moloto. Why do I say this? Well, because we in the courtroom are all aware of the schedule planned for the Prosecution case which shows that the case will be a lengthy one because of the testimony and the transcripts that we have to deal with and the voluminous documents that will be tendered into evidence, or that we expect to be tendered into evidence. And, secondly, Your Honours, you are well aware of the fact that this Defence team was formed fairly rapidly immediately prior to the commencement of the trial. We've really been doing our utmost to keep up with everything, and this was perhaps not possible in the pre-trial phase. We've been doing everything we can to deal with the trial. I have to say that the fact that we had a break in October has been of assistance to us, and the fact that we're not sitting on Friday is also of assistance because we really don't have a single weekend that we can use for rest, and I can say this quite openly. I don't expect that this team will be able to rest for a single day even in the course of the Christmas period; and in the course of the summer, regardless of the stage we arrive at, I think we will be working continually in order to prepare for the Defence case. But given the means at our disposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, Mr. Lukic. We've moved a little far away from what we're talking about. We're talking about the 98 bis now. Can I suggest that you come back to the Chamber with what you suggest would be a reasonable time for the -- to give you time to prepare. That's the proposal of the Chamber. I would like you to come back with your proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comments to make on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our view, Your Honour, is that the submissions should be oral, and it should not be lengthy written proceedings on 98 bis. Furthermore, we do not believe that the protracted break is necessary, given the case is being analysed on an ongoing basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might say one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take your suggestion in mind and I don't disagree with Mr. Harmon with regard to the fact that the case is being analysed on an ongoing basis. However, one of the things that is true, which is what I think Mr. Lukic was getting to - and I will not take a long time - is that most of the people who are working with us right now and who are supporting us are interns and they will be gone. So we will be losing a fair amount of our team, and we don't have, unfortunately, the continuity of history that exists for the Prosecution. So with regard to the analysis that's going on, we're in a constant -- we're in a constant process of having to educate people as well. I'm just putting that on the record so you can appreciate now one of our concerns. But we will get back to you with regard to when an appropriate amount of time would be -- or what an appropriate amount of time would be, in our estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Let me reserve my comments. Okay. Let's call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you begin by stating your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Robert J. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to try and deal with our presentation today thematically, and the first area I'd like to deal with will be your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please call up in that regard 65 ter number 9212, 09212. We're re-releasing that document now, Your Honour, and my apologies. We've worked very hard to have the technology in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you still fail.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only a bump in the road, one might say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you receiving anything, Madam Registrar, because we've re-released again 9212. It may be something that we actually have no control over, Your Honour. Let's see if we can explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to go to the old and trusted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm ready to go to the old and trusted, but we've been saved by the technological gods, I'm advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a copy of the document on the screen in front of you, one in English and one in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us, is there any recent work or affiliations to your curriculum vitae that is not contained in here that you feel the Trial Chamber should be aware of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Two. One is merely a continuation of a previous appointment, but beginning in -- beginning again in January of 2009, I will be serving as Visiting Professor of History at the University of Michigan; and, second, I was elected to the -- as a Corresponding Member of the Academy of Sciences -- Arts and Sciences of Bosnia and Herzegovina about three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to this second item you referred to, Corresponding Member of the Academy of Arts and Sciences of Bosnia and Herzegovina, can you tell us what that means effectively?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is a recognition essentially of a level of scholarly achievement to which is bestowed on perhaps several dozen scholars who are from Bosnia-Herzegovina or have worked on topics related to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with these modifications or updates you've just spoken about, could you otherwise confirm the accuracy of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With that, Your Honour, could I ask this be admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to continue further, and perhaps we don't need to erase that document from the screen because we may go back to it as we deal with this theme, could I ask you, sir, how would you describe your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm an independent historian and consultant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you have in that field any area of specialisation in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. My historical training and work is principally in the history of the lands of the former Yugoslavia in the nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first centuries, mainly social, political, and, to a lesser degree, military history of those lands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in respect to those lands of the former Yugoslavia, do you consider yourself as having any more detailed focus or specialisation in any one of those lands in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Most of my work is on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as a historian, what do you do? What does your craft consist of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Principally writing history and also disseminating historical knowledge through lectures, seminars, conferences, presentations to various groups that need it for preparation of one sort or another for their occupational work.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have a long-standing interest in the history of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How far does that interest date back?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It dates back to 1965 when I attended a summer seminar in Yugoslavia and then remained for a semester of study at the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, where I read history with two mentors at the -- in the history department at the University of Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, if my math is correct, that's more than 40 years.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any dealing with Bosnia and Herzegovina in particular now? Do you have any family or other ties to the region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I have no ethnic or family ties to the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you frequently travelled there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you continue to do so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Three to four times a year for the past 14 years anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Always now in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, have you conducted research there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what types of institutions or organs have you conducted research at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Principally the archives, various archives, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily in Sarajevo but also in other cities and towns of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in addition to information, documentation, about that region housed in archives in Belgrade, Zagreb, Budapest, Vienna, and London.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any command of the Serbo-Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would characterise my speaking command of it as very good, my reading command of it as very good, and my writing of it is good.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you previously produced reports for this Tribunal in connection with events in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I believe the list of them is at -- toward the end of my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I've testified on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you ever been asked by any Defence team to testify in a case before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I've never been approached to either testify or prepare a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you taught social and political history of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's been part of my teaching work at the University of Michigan in the last several years and also part of my teaching in the late 1980s -- I'm sorry, 1970s, from about 1975 to 1981, at both the university -- Ohio State University and the University of Oregon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I see from your curriculum vitae you lecture on the same subject. How recently have you done that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I give lectures frequently to various audiences. I recently did it ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is that nationally or internationally? And by "nationally," I'm referring to the United States, given that I see you're an American resident.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I've lectured at a wide variety of universities in the United States, or given a lecture, and given conference papers and reports at conferences and universities in Sarajevo, Belgrade, Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note also in your CV there's a heading called "Peace-keeping Training," and that's on page 5 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S. I note there you provide briefings for American military units heading to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosovo as a part of SFOR and KFOR. What do those briefings include?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They consist a broad historical introduction -- historical and cultural introduction to Bosnia and/or Kosovo, as the case may be appropriate, designed for the command element of the unit that's being dispatched as a part of those UN-sanctioned peace-keeping forces. The one in Bosnia is no longer SFOR. That was dissolved in 2004. The American contribution to that is now limited to a NATO headquarters in Sarajevo. So that group is much smaller and consists of a small part of the overall NATO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Thank you very much. We talked a few minutes ago about reports you produced for the Tribunal. Have you produced reports on or relating to the social and political history of Bosnia-Herzegovina for any other outside organisations or agencies or governments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared a report for the Canadian Department of Justice, and occasionally prepare reports and make presentations for the US Department of State.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just a question about your dealings with the Yugoslav community generally and perhaps the scholarly community. Have you had dealings with the Serbian academic community during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Oh, I certainly have. My initial research venture to Sarajevo, the full year of research that I did from 1974 to 1975, I worked under the mentorship of Professor Milorad Macic, who was a prominent Serbian historian, then living in Sarajevo, and a member of the Academy of Sciences of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time and of -- now of the Serbian Academy of Sciences. I attended a conference in Belgrade two years ago and had quite a lot of dealings with -- discussions with Serbian historians there, and pay a lot of attention to the literature that comes out of the community of Serbian historians, both in Serbia itself and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I've also edited and written an introduction for a book by a Bosnian Serb which is listed on my CV.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From the names on your CV, I would guess that -- or I would suppose that would be the book entitled "Political Memoirs of a Bosnian Serb"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By an individual by the name of Mirko Pejnovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Pejnovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Mr. Pejnovic is today the Dean of the Faculty of Political Science at the University of Sarajevo. During the period from June 1992 until summer of 1994, he was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just relating to books, I see you're a published author; and those books which are noted on page 1 of your CV, have they received critical recognition from the Yugoslav community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. All of them have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From -- including from the Serbian community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: From Serbs and -- yes, from Serbs from -- it has received critical assessment, indeed, from many different historians and reviewers of all ethnicities in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm unclear what the term "critical" means. It's a word that has a number of different tones and shades. It could be critical from the standpoint of disapproval. It could be critical from the standpoint of an incisive understanding of what the author in this particular situation has produced. I just wonder if we can get some clarification with regard to that issue so it doesn't hang in the air as a vagary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. Perhaps I could ask another question in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These books that you've written, are you aware as to whether they've received -- as to whether they've been positively accepted by the Yugoslav scholarly community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there's no Yugoslav scholarly community today, so I don't know that I could answer that at that level. It has been positive -- they have been positively received by scholars from Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian Muslim or Bosniak provenance, but not unanimously by any group.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And speaking of the groups, does that apply to groups who are resident in the United States as well as groups who are resident in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Reviews from all those groups have been largely positive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, is Mr. Guy-Smith to understand that "critical" means positive?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In -- that was my original intention, and I strove to clarify that with the later question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you wanted to ask the witness was whether his books had been critiqued, which is different from criticised.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move on to the two reports which form the basis of your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I would like to ask Madam Registrar to call them up so that Dr. Donia can see the first page of those reports, the first one being 65 ter number 02169.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see this next document on the screen in front of you in English and in B/C/S as well now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I prepared in 2002 for the -- under a commission from the Prosecution for the trial of Mr. Krajisnik. I believe I testified about this report further in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on to the next report, again I only need the first page displayed. That would be 65 ter number 02290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there anything you would like to do with this 65 ter document before we move on to the next one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Taking in mind Your Honours' guidelines from your decision on the report of Dr. Donia, I would like to deal with that at the end of his testimony, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. 02290 is the next 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report that I prepared for the Prosecution in the case of Mr. Dragomir Milosevic in 2006, and was questioned about this report in July of 2007 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry. March of 2007, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just, for the record, could you tell us the title of this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: "From Elections to Stalemate: The Making of the Sarajevo Siege, 1990-1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I omitted for the record to ask for the title of your -- the first report that was displayed for you, 65 ter 02169. Do you recall the title?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. Could we have it displayed again, please, 02169, just for completeness of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The Origins of Republika Srpska, 1990-1992 - A Background Report."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that these reports were prepared as a result of -- on a commission from the Prosecution in those cases. Do you recall whether they were prepared as a result of some kind of written mandate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Neither one of these reports was prepared in response to a written mandate, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were the objectives, then, of these reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I was asked by the Prosecution to prepare a report which explained and enlightened the background of the major developments, events, and institutions referenced in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From that, then, perhaps I could take you one step further and ask if you could describe, then, the nature of these two reports. Are they similar in nature or dissimilar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They are similar in their fundamental structure. Each is an empirically based narrative account, topically organised, of the major developments and institutions pertaining to these two topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you go about preparing, then? Is there any theoretical approach or a methodology that underlines the way you prepared these reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The method of preparation is essentially one of interaction between myself as a writer and the documents on which the account is based. Now, I say "interactive" in the sense that I seek always to try to -- I have sought in these reports to take into account a very broad spectrum of information and documentation, and to then formulate the specific narrative in response to the best available documentation and the density of that documentation, the verifiability of it, the richness of the documentary record, and, the, let's say, the independence of that -- the reliability of the sources. There is, furthermore, a viewpoint, or perhaps one could call it a theory, underpinning these reports which is the view that nationalities and national movements are constructed entities, rather than primordial ones. That is a debate that has flourished in a number of disciplines over the past perhaps three decades, with the view that I share being that ethnic groups and national movements are dynamic, constantly changing phenomena that will mutate over time, depending on the actions of the elites that form them and lead them. So they're very much contemporary human creations, as opposed to those people who see them primordial, ever-lasting entities. What that means in practice is that I reject the often-seen national accounts by Bosnian Muslims, Serbs, or Croats that everything that happened was just a re-run of something from the Middle Ages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go back to methodology in a different way, you mentioned the broad base of material you deal with. What's your criteria for selecting the documents from this broad base of material that you use to write your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, relevance. It has to actually apply directly to the narrative that I'm writing; second, reliability, either as determined by internal content of the document and/or external assessments of the source of the document; third would be its inter-connectability, its verifiability, consistency with other documents of the time and source; and, finally, richness. I think the value of the document, its appropriateness to be included as a citation or even quoted, depends on its ability to illuminate the topic that I'm addressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you determine reliability? How do you make an assessment of a document's reliability?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there are two ways one can do that. I think one does that, and that is, first of all, to look at the source. The words of an actor in a particular event clearly bear more weight and have greater validity than the words of a third- or fourth-hand person or someone who is not in a position to directly observe events. So that character of the source is the first important thing. Then the second important thing would be the assessment of -- from the outside of the value of the value of document from other documents and sources that were generated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just in terms of sources, then, going back again to these reports, can you outline what collections and selections you relied on for the preparation of these reports, dealing first with the report entitled "Origins of the Republika Srpska"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think I could probably address the two of them together. It is voluminous. It consists of a survey that I have made over the years of the periodical press from several different publications in several different parts of the former Yugoslavia, surveys of documentation that I've been either provided by the Office of the Prosecutor or have gleaned from those documents put into evidence in other cases, documents from the United Nations and other international organisations, and those people who've had first-hand accounts of events there. It's a very voluminous collection of documents that constitutes, let's say, the base from which the reports were prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, more specifically, I note that your first report, "The Origins of the Republika Srpska," and to a lesser extent, but it also refers in your second report, but you refer to transcripts of sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the RS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's a key source of information and evidence in the report on the "Origins of the Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a historian, what relevance was that collection to the preparation of these reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is, as far as I have been able to identify, the best collection of the thinking and expressions of intent by the Bosnian Serb nationalist leadership, leaders, that I have found. Many of the sessions were held under the presumption of confidentiality. Others were not but many of them were, and, consequently, many of the expressions appear to be remarkably candid. So it's a very valuable source, and I would rate it at the top, really, or near the top of the available sources about the making of the Republika Srpska, particularly the thinking and attitudes of those who actually did the creating.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your second report, "The Making of the Siege of Sarajevo," there was, in fact -- or I saw, in fact, some evidence of other or additional sources you consulted that weren't noted in the first report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that would be true, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you speak to those sources. What did you consult?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I consulted the United Nations reports, the reports of the newspaper -- principally the newspaper Oslobodjenje which was published continuously during the war within the city of Sarajevo, the interviews that I conducted with a number of participants and leaders, and, additionally, some of the documentation that was provided to me by the Office of the Prosecutor regarding some of the activities before the war in various municipalities of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note, in this last answer, you've stipulated that you consulted newspaper reports, principally the newspaper Oslobodjenje. As a historian, what value or relevance do you attribute to this periodic press from the time period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The periodical press from that time has, I think, a particular value for a couple reasons. Number one, in the socialist period, all these newspapers had a founding organisation, either the municipality or the city of Sarajevo or even the League of Communists, and, as such, was mandated to be a newspaper of record. Journalists and editors maintained that commitment to be a newspaper of record even as they developed some very opinionated content on their editorial page. Second, we have in the periodical press a lot of on-site investigative reporting. People who were trained to note with their eyes and ears what took place, who said what, and how to pen it in a way that conveyed to a reader the genuine sense of what the atmosphere was like and what the players said, are just throughout the periodical press of not only Sarajevo but Banja Luka and even newspapers from outside the Bosnia -- outside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have two questions based on that. First of all, what's a "newspaper of record"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: A newspaper of record notion is that the newspaper will print, often without editing, a press release, a speech, the content of a resolution or memorandum, in its columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, to go back to the question I initially asked you, as a historian, then, what value do you place on this periodic press you described from this period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it does, really, for me two things. It gives me a great deal of insight into not just what happened but how it happened, why it happened, what the thinking of the actors was. And, second, it gives me a sense of sequence and progression because a newspaper typically follows a story for many days, weeks, or even years; and, consequently, it's a very solid source of the evolution of people's thinking or the institutions and players that were examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll move on to some areas more directly linked to portions of your report?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But at this stage and with my friend Mr. Guy-Smith's -- subject to my friend Mr. Guy-Smith's permission, I'd like to offer Dr. Donia copies of these reports as they were filed with my friend in the Chambers, so that he might have them to refer to them during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. Wonderful idea. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Registrar. Two copies go to Dr. Donia; that is, two reports, one copy of each. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now to begin, I'd like to go to the report on the "Origins of the Republika Srpska," pages 20 and 21 in English and 18 and 19 in B/C/S. There you make note of the differing views of the nationalist parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period leading up to the multi-party elections as regards the nature of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's relationship to Yugoslavia. Have you found that -- those passages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to explain the SDS party's view in this regard, in regard to the nature of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's relationship to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to continue to be part of a federal Yugoslav state with the goal of strengthening the federation; that is, they wanted either the status quo or stronger links between the various federal states and the centre. The SDS did have a backup position in the event that Yugoslavia disintegrated or federal Yugoslavia ceased to exist. In their view, they wished to be part of a Serbian state, a state in which all Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Two questions. One I should have asked you a little bit earlier. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, what was the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The SDS was the party of the Serbian Democratic Party, Stranka Demokratske Akcije, which was formed in July of 1990 to compete in the first multi-party elections, democratic elections, in November of that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "Serbian Democratic Party," it's the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. There was an SDS of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was the head of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic was its president.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to go back to the position you've articulated, it seems to contemplate two possibilities; and I'd just like to know, were they always expressed as backup or alternative possibilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I would ask that Ms. Edgerton pay attention to what is potentially is a leading question. She can ask what was the various positions as opposed to suggesting an answer as to where she wants to go. I'm asking for caution more than for an actual objection yet in terms of a totally leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. Yes, Your Honour, I can go back to page 23, line 12, where Dr. Donia noted: "The SDS did have a backup position to their first option," and ask the question this way: Dr. Donia, you said earlier that the SDS's backup position in the event Yugoslavia disintegrated or a federal Yugoslavia ceased to exist was that the SDS wished to be part of a Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd simply like to know: Is that how the relationship or the envision of the relationship was always expressed, as a backup.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was expressed as a backup until such time as it appeared that federal Yugoslavia was in disintegration and would not survive or would be transformed. That came in very late 1991, perhaps late December 1991, and the early couple of months of 1992. At that point, the first option having become unviable, the second backup solution became the first one, really. The other thing to be said, I think, is that the backup, option B, was less clearly -- there was less agreement on exactly the form of that backup option among the Bosnian Serb leaders and Serb leaders generally than there was about the initial position about maintaining federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could explore the articulations of these notions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that regard, could I call up 65 ter 6686, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see a document in Cyrillic and one in English on your screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was a document prepared in November of 1990, just after the declaration of the creation of the Serbian National Council in which the -- Karadzic spelled out the fundamental position of the party toward Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I take us all down to heading III, which is the bottom of the first page in English, and I think -- yes. It appears in part on the bottom of the first page in Serbo-Croatian, and then we'll have to go over to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could you have a look at the heading III, which begins with the sentence "The will of the Serbian people ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And tell me if you have any comment with regard to this statement based on your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Karadzic here essentially articulates the position that the federal unit is necessary based on the notion that Bosnia-Herzegovina consists of sovereign peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this statement in paragraph III consistent with what you've articulated as being the position of the SDS as regards the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's relationship with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The second part of this -- well, part III and paragraph IV go into, in rather vague terms, the backup option to which I've referred; that is, what would happen to Serbs should federal Yugoslavia cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just a bit unclear. I take it that what the witness is doing is interpreting the paragraph, and the reason I'm asking the question is because I'm not seeing the language of "sovereign people." I see "sovereign and equal nations" and I see "the Serbian people," and I see "Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and other nations." I'm just curious as to whether or not what we're having occur here is an interpretation of the document, or whether or not he is indicating that this is, in fact, what the document itself says. Just so I'm clear. I'm trying to make sure that I understand precisely what the witness is alluding to here, since he used the term "essentially," and considering that we're dealing with the issue of, as the witness put it, concerns about what I will call the primordial nature of the human being. I'm sure he's appreciative of the distinction between peoples and nations. I want to make sure that our language is somewhat specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can clarify this with the witness now, if Your Honour wishes; but, properly, I would submit it's a matter that Mr. Guy-Smith can raise in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just trying to make life easy. I'm happy to do it the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Because, in fact, you're really not objecting. You are wanting to tell the witness what words to use, which I find a little difficult, and I think you can clarify that in cross-examination, Mr. Guy-Smith. If you see any fundamental difference between the word "peoples" and "nations," it's a matter for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this notion that you've described, Dr. Donia, as articulated in 6686 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, before I forget myself, Your Honours, could I ask that 6686 be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this notion that we've -- you've described, Dr. Donia, and we've seen articulated in Exhibit P325, have you seen evidence in your research that would illustrate this notion was common to both SDS leaders and authorities in power in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- I've seen several speeches or statements by President Milosevic that take essentially the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 2247.07, please, 2247.07. This document, for everyone's information, is an extract, page 28, from a book by Srdjan Radulovic, entitled "Sudbina Krajine."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, what does "Sudbina Krajine" mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Fate of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, are you familiar with Srdjan Radulovic is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a journalist/correspondent who covered the developments in Croatia in 1990, 1991, I believe for the newspaper Politika. I'm not sure of the newspaper that he worked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the B/C/S copy, the paragraph I'd like to bring your attention to is the final paragraph on the page; and in the English translation, I'd like you to go, please, to page 3. But now, unfortunately, we have -- or I have two English page 3s on my screen, so if you can try and keep the B/C/S one on the screen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I'd like to take your attention to the paragraph at the top of this page 3 of the English translation, where you see reference to a statement by Slobodan Milosevic on -- at an enlarged session of the Presidency on the eve of the Serbian elections.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you have a look at that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note this is a document you referred to in your report. Do you have any comment on whether this statement by Slobodan Milosevic is consistent with the notion that you've described as being held by the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In this statement, Milosevic says that the first -- the preferred solution is a democratic federation. He also addresses a backup alternative to that, which he articulates as this very widely used slogan, "the Serbian people want to live in a single state." He, in this manner, doesn't, as I said, be terribly precise about what that alternative means, but it's clear that the -- that's the alternative in the event that a federation is not accepted by other parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I submit this, please, as a further Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is made as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on, please, to 65 ter number 2234. And in the Serbo-Croatian version that's on the right-hand side of the screen, the item to highlight is the paragraph in the box on the top left-hand corner that mentions the word "Poker." Sorry, top left-hand corner. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a page from the Banja Luka newspaper Glas, or Voice, which was the probably second most widely read newspaper in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that time, based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the English translation of the article entitled "Otvoreni Poker," I'd like us to go down towards the bottom of page 1, two-thirds of the way down. I'd like you to look at the sentence that begins with -- it's a little more than two-thirds of the way down in the English. It begins with "According to Karadzic ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you could have a look at that sentence and then please indicate to Mr. Registrar when you're prepared to go over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, the B/C/S -- corresponding B/C/S paragraph should be just on the left-hand side. Thank you. It's a bit difficult to describe, but it's almost opposite the bolded part on the right-hand side of the page, and it begins with the sentence "Svi Srbi." Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just at the top of your screen.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. "According to Karadzic, all Serbs have one goal, which is to live in a common state." He is here expressing the, I would say, overall objective Serbs, preferably within Yugoslavia. Then he expresses the backup goal, which is then in a Greater Serbia. Just to emphasise, these are -- this is a description provided by the journalist Gordan Truhelj, who is a veteran journalist covering political developments in Bosnian Krajina. His analysis of this was to note that the Greater Serbia option was put forward at the meeting, first presented as an official choice and then - go to the next page - always presented as an alternative to Yugoslavia, as I have said. But clearly stated, this relationship between the decline of the Yugoslav option, should that occur, the more viable the option of a Greater Serbia would be. These are the observations of the journalist on this speech of Karadzic in Banja Luka two days before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attribute any particular significance to this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is a report on an unusual speech, in that the term "Greater Serbia" and the notion of Greater Serbia was openly presented by Karadzic; and the occasion itself which involves Serbs from Knin, from the Krajina in Croatia, were a part of the rally. I think this is a good analysis of the relationship between these options in the description of this experience of, I think, a perceptive journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask, please, that this be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could move forward in time from there to events in October 1991, which you referred to in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to ask, since it looks like you're moving into a slightly new topic, wouldn't that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I apologise for not noting the time; but, indeed, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take the break, then, and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, what I'd like to do is move forward in time now to an Assembly session of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the middle of October 1991, a session that actually began at the end of the first week of October and culminated in events on the night of the 15th of October. Are you familiar with this session?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not it was televised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to see the broadcast or later copies of the broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I've seen both the videotape of the proceedings -- I did not see the broadcast at the time it was transmitted, but I've seen a videotape of it since then and transcripts of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you followed media reports, printed media reports, of events that took place that night?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I've examined a number of media reports of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, then, in a nutshell, in summary fashion, what happened that night? Was it a significant night for the republic as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a watershed event, I think, in most people's assessment, and mine as well. The session had been convened to arrive at a negotiating position for Bosnia-Herzegovina in peace talks then underway in The Hague with the aim of ending the war in Croatia. Several groups presented draft resolutions defining the platform for those negotiations and a memorandum of sovereignty which was presented by the HDZ and SDA leaders. In the course of the long debates of the evening of the 14th of October, Radovan Karadzic made a particularly pointed speech that aroused a great deal of response in the other delegates present. Subsequent to that speech, the chairman of the -- or president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, dissolved the Assembly -- I'm sorry, not dissolved, but adjourned the Assembly. Then Mariofil Ljubic, who was the vice-president of the Assembly, reconvened it with the delegates of the SDA and HDZ only remaining in the auditorium. They subsequently passed a memorandum of sovereignty and a platform which expressed those parties' approach to the negotiations and, as a part of that, the nature of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to go back now to develop some of the points you've made in this summary, could you explain, first of all, who the organs you've described -- sorry, let me ask you the question this way: If you go back to page 33, line 12, you mentioned HDZ and SDA leaders. What was the HDZ and what was the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These were two national parties that were founded in the summer of 1990 in preparation for the November elections. The HDZ was the Croatian Democratic Community. It drew votes almost exclusively from Croatian -- Bosnians of Croatian nationality, bore the same name as a party in Croatia itself. The SDA was the Party of Democratic Action. It appealed to and drew votes from almost exclusively Bosnian Muslim constituents. It was headed by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this platform and memorandum you've mentioned, are you familiar with those two documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then ask that 65 ter 9122 be displayed, please, 9122. Would you re-release, please. We'll just wait for a moment until the original - there we go - is loaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you see the documents on the screen in front of you, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the B/C/S document that you see in front of you is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The B/C/S document is a page from Oslobodjenje of 15 October 1991 which carries a story in the upper left-hand corner about the session itself. And in the right-hand two columns, it carries the text of proposed resolutions submitted by the three principal contenders in this discussion. At the top the -- I can't see it quite clearly --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you think you could enlarge the box in the B/C/S on the top right-hand corner, which begins with the title "Za Suverenu BiH."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue. Have I asked them to enlarge the article you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the draft memorandum of the SDA and HDZ which was passed with, as far as I can tell, no significant changes, in that, at about 2.30 in the morning on the 15th of October, the document that we're looking at is the memorandum. As I indicated, there was a separate document which was the platform for the negotiating position of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this memorandum articulates the position of these two parties, and then after the vote of the Assembly, that the future arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina must include the Serbian and Croatian republics, and that Bosnia must be -- must have its relations with both in the same manner. It also states that the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina will not attend sessions of the federal Yugoslav institutions that are not attended by representatives of all other republics. In the first paragraph, it cites Amendment 60 to the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was passed in February 1990, and made this nuanced but very significant change in the constitutional formulation to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of equal citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this formulation that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of equal citizens, in your mind, consistent with the notion of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. It was diametrically opposed to it. The point becomes very clear when you look at the wording of the platform in which the -- these two parties adopt the position that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a civic state, that is, a state of its citizens, without reference to the sovereignty of its peoples, and, therefore, should be governed by majority rule and equal rights for all citizens, as opposed to the SDS position that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state of three sovereign peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I move on, could I ask that this document be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we turn now to 65 ter number 09009.01, which, for everyone's information, is a transcript of the speech that Mr. Karadzic made which this witness has referred to earlier. Your indulgence for a moment while I make a note, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this speech, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic's speech to the Assembly in the early hours of 15 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you found in this speech reflections of the view that you've just articulated in page 36, lines 10 and 11, that the SDS position was that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state of three sovereign peoples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm having trouble seeing the full English page here. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please. Could we scroll down in the English copy, please, and then in the B/C/S copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. About halfway through the last paragraph on that page in the English, which the sentence begins with the word "But ..." which is in about line 7: "But you have no way to get it, nor have you the way to realise it later on, because all people are sovereign, Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, for the record, the B/C/S of that sentence is in approximately the same position in the last paragraph, halfway through; and if I'm not mistaken, it begins with the sentence "Nemate nikakgov nacina ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we scroll over to the next page, please, to give Dr. Donia an opportunity to review the document in full.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to go to a sentence that's in the bottom -- about the bottom half of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Bottom half of the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Bottom half of the page as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Bottom of the first paragraph is good, in this section that begins: "And one of the most flagrant things in all that you are doing is that you are trying to describe the acts of Slovenia and Croatia as legal." He then goes on to accuse the rival parties of wanting to see Slovenia and Croatia become independent in hopes that the Croats and Muslims of Bosnia would be dragged along.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you interpret anything from this remark?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he believes that the -- he is alleging that the Muslims and Croats, with this resolution, are going to follow the course toward independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps I can ask you a question by taking us over to the next page, number 3, of both the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Approximately halfway down the page, just over halfway down the page in both documents, if you can stop with the scrolling in the English, I'll just take a moment to find it. When it's one whole paragraph per page, Your Honour, you can appreciate it's somewhat difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The sentence in any case in the English version begins with: "You want to achieve in The Hague ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at that sentence, which continues down -- or that passage, which continues down to the sentence which ends with"... not for other people as well." And while you do that, I'll try and identify where this provision is in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think this is one of the clearest articulations of this principal so strongly held to by Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders that the sovereignty of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the predominant principle that should govern political life. "You want to achieve in The Hague," and I'll just go down to the sentence that says: "Sovereign people in Bosnia and Herzegovina can each say for themselves what they want, but not for other people as well. It was one of the conclusions made in this Assembly." There's a statement that these are -- the peoples are essentially billiard ball type objects with -- they're completely self-contained and cannot have any influence on other peoples because of their sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could ask your assistance, Mr. Registrar. In the B/C/S version, could you scroll up in the page, because I don't see that passage displayed just yet. If you could stop now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, because of your facility in the language, perhaps you could assist us in identifying the same passage for the record in this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does it begin with the sentence, "Vi hocete u Haagu ..." on --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just not able to put my finger on this immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, for this, but I'm aiming for precision as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. "Mr. Izetbegovic in The Hague is --" strike that. The sentence that says "Suvereni norodi u Bosni i Herzegovini" is part of the passage. If you see "Sovereign people in Bosnia-Herzegovina can each say for themselves what they want," which I just cited, that is in the B/C/S about one-third of the way down this page, as it's currently displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Donia. Now, just one further question about this transcript, or, generally speaking, your recollection of the session, you mentioned earlier that Dr. Karadzic made a pointed speech. Do you recall him saying anything that incurred a public reaction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. His next to last thought paragraph in this speech ended with a very pointed exclamation or statement about the possibility of the extinguishing of the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next exhibit, could I please ask that this document be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now with everyone's indulgence, I would like to play the transcript of -- to play the video of the portion that Dr. Donia has just referred to. This will be played in Sanction, Your Honours; and for the sake of the record, we'll only be seeing the English version of what the speaker's saying on the Sanction programme. So I'm wondering if I could ask, and this is a very short clip, I'm wondering if I could ask the indulgence of our colleagues in the interpreters booth to read out the English so we have a full record, an appropriate record, of what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure they heard you. I see they are nodding.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please play the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You want in The Hague to achieve for this to be the third or fourth republic which will not stay in Yugoslavia. I'm sorry, but we want to stay in Yugoslavia. You can speak only for yourself. Sovereign people in Bosnia-Herzegovina can each say for themselves what they want, but not for other people as well. It was one of the conclusions made by this Assembly. We shall disable you to carry out violence against Serbian people, constitutional violence, in front of local and international public, because after -- we won't be consulted if we come into the situation in which Slovenia and Croatia are in, especially Croatia, knowing that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the hell would be 1.000 times worse than there. "I have to send this message to all the delegates. Gentlemen, believe me, even if you would make something tonight, even though you have no way of making it, because we have the constitutional manner to prevent you from voting. But even if you would make something, that would be the source of shame for Mr. Izetbegovic and in The Hague. It would also be a great shame for the image of this parliament in Europe and for all these peoples in Yugoslavia and Europe. It would be especially your embarrassment, Croats and Muslims, who are loyal to this idea, your shame and your proof of how much you respect sovereignty and equality of Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "I am asking you one more time - I am not threatening, I'm asking - to take seriously the interpretation of the political will of Serbian people, which is represented here by the Serbian Democratic Party and Serbian Movement of Renewal, and several Serbs from some other parties. Please do take it seriously. This is not good, what you are doing. This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people in possible extinction, because Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you mentioned earlier that you had an opportunity to review the videotape of the telecast; and towards the end of this topic in your testimony, you recalled Dr. Karadzic's statement about the possibility of the extinguishing of the Bosnian Muslims. Is this the statement you recall having reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have an administrative question which I would ask Your Honours' guidance on. I'd like to ask this be marked as an exhibit, but I think it would make sense, subject to Your Honours, of course, that this be marked somehow as part of P329 so that they are, for everybody's sake, cross-referenced and can easily be associated, if that's at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, it's been suggested by Madam Registrar that she could either make it P329.1 or just cross-reference it, whatever you prefer. Make your pick.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, given the way we all have to search through the systems, it would probably be more convenient down the road for it to be called 329.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will become Exhibit P329.1, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what's the 65 ter number of that clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of the clip, it's 65 ter number 9009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's given the number P329.1. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to move on, and this is noted in your report on the making of the Sarajevo siege, pages 9 of the English and 10 of the B/C/S translation, to move on to what you've noted as the SDS Party Council meeting which took place after this speech. Could I ask you, who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The key elected leaders of the SDS, Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, and a number of members of the body that was designated the Party Council, I sometimes see it as the Political Council, who were not involved in the daily SDS affairs but viewed as intellectuals with particular insight and contributions to make to the overall direction that the party should take.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before you go further, could I ask for 65 ter number 2223, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, before the document finally comes up, I could ask you this: Are you in a position to give further detail to the Trial Chamber about what the SDS Party Council was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think I've just given about what I can. It is, in some sense, an advisory body that was listened to very closely because of its composition, prominent intellectuals and political activists in the party. Its chairman Slavko Lejovac was a member of the Academy of Sciences in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a professor. So that's the intellectual component of it. Milorad Ekmecic who, of course, was my former mentor in the 1970s, was also one of those prominent intellectuals who was on the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the documents on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These are the English translation and B/C/S original of notes or minutes taken at the meeting of 15th October 1991, that is, the evening after the morning -- the evening of the same day in which the actions were approved in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina at 2.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to your mind, did this meeting have any significance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's very significant in that it effectively launched the party on a course toward a separate Bosnian Serb national polity and outlined the steps to be taken in that direction. The suggestions come from individual participants. The notes do not show any conclusions reached, nor was there, to my knowledge, any public announcement of conclusions, but the individual actions proposed were, in many cases, implemented within a matter of days or weeks after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Individual actions such as?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, if I could look at Professor Ekmecic's contribution, for example, he proposes that the regions that have already been created, by which he refers to the SAOs, the Serbian autonomous areas, should not be allowed to form their own separate governments, but should be linked into a single state headquartered in Sarajevo. There --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down the page first, and then over to the next page until we see the name of Dr. Koljevic at the very top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Koljevic advocates a plebiscite and taking a plebiscite immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does Mr. Ostojic advocate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He suggests that SDS representatives in power should consider -- should be permitted to withdraw if they wish, and that the party go into a formal opposition position. He also wants to ask the two parties that passed the resolution to suspend their decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic was -- became the Minister of Information in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was a specialist for media working in the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, were these recommendations that you've listed among the actions that took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere in here also is a recommendation for the establishment of an assembly, a separate body. Well, at point 2 here, just before Dr. Karadzic speaks, "create a parallel body of authority which would primarily be reflected in the creation of a Serbian parliament." That step was taken on October 24th, 1991.
