A referendum was -- the Serb leaders organised a referendum for the 9th and 10th of November, 1991; and in December, took steps towards formation of a separate Serb polity within Bosnia-Herzegovina, a step which they formalised on the 9th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, then, before moving on, could I ask that this document be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've noted the founding of -- you've noted the creation of a Serb parliament on 24 October 1991, lines 10 and 11 of page46. Was that what you called as a parliament actually called a Serb parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was first known as the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It subsequently was renamed in -- sometime in late summer of 1992 as the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter number 2071 be produced, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is not an objection. This is a request that when Ms. Edgerton is asking questions concerning the Bosnian Serb parliament or the founding of such an institution, that she identifies it as being a Bosnian Serb parliament, because the word "Serb" and the potential connotation of such a word has far-reaching consequences; and since we're trying to identify a specific group, I'd appreciate that. The answer, obviously, discusses a Bosnian Serb parliament, but the term "Serb" has a great deal of meaning and can go far, and I'm just asking that that be done in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, I'll take it on, Your Honour. I was only using the words of the witness, which is why I referred to the page and line numbers; but, of course, I'll take it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 2071, I believe was the 65 ter number I asked for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the documents that appear on your screen, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These are excerpts from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I ask for your indulgence, Your Honour. I think we have a document displayed that I didn't intend to be displayed. Your indulgence. I should note this is because, Your Honour, we've got a number of translations and revised translations and excerpts, and I'll be more specific in identifying the one I want displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The one you now want is not 2071?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. The one I want, Your Honour, is actually 2071.02, in English, and the original is also 2071.02. My apologies, Your Honour. No. Your Honour, we'll move on because I don't wish to take the Court's time while we work through this; and if it's a point that needs to be come back to, with everyone's permission, I'll come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, now that we've come to the founding of the Assembly of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'd like to revert back to the theme we were discussing earlier in your testimony, which was the SDS notion of the nature of the relation that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have with Yugoslavia, and ask you whether you found in your continued research, in connection with these reports and otherwise, evidence of continued SDS support for this notion? That's because I'm dating it in time now. Now the Assembly of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been established. So within the Assembly, have you found evidence of continued SDS support for this notion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, then, 65 ter number 2079 be called up, and just your indulgence again for a moment, Your Honour. Once it's called up, I'll be able to direct us to the appropriate page. 2079. If you go to page 62, please, in the English, and pages 78 and 79 of the Serbo-Croatian. The Serbo-Croatian is correct, and I'm just going to get you the exact page. Just to put it in context, Your Honour, the difficulty I might run into, and I hope it doesn't come up frequently at all, is because we've obtained CLSS translations of the display paragraphs, in the event there was need to refer to those. So sometimes I need to distinguish between one translation and the other one. Your indulgence for a moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see everything is displayed appropriately here now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I direct you to the part on page 78 of the B/C/S and the bottom of page 62, where you see -- where you see Momcilo Krajisnik speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to the next paragraph on both of those pages -- sorry, if we could continue on to the next pages. Now, on page 62, which is now displayed in English, please go down to the paragraph on the bottom which begins: "Gentlemen, if we succeed in completing a federal BiH ..." Keep going. Thank you. The same paragraph is now displayed on the screen, and it is the last paragraph on page 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I apologise for the preamble, but if you could look at this quotation of Mr. Krajisnik's, which begins with, "... if we succeed in creating a federal BiH ..." and ends with "... the Serbian people should be united more than now than ever before ..." Perhaps I could ask you this: Is this some evidence of continued support for the notion we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he can -- the witness can tell us what it is. The notion that -- the question, as framed, is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith--

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Some evidence," I mean, he can explain what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you know, we're having here an expert witness who is being called upon to give his opinion. He is here to give opinion evidence. I'm not quite sure what you mean by she's leading. He's following --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can explain to you precisely what I mean, if you want, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like me to finish what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please let me. The witness has been explaining a particular theme that he says he's identified in the speeches of various speakers in the SDS, and what he's being asked is whether he can pick up the same theme here. This answer is going to be, Yes, it's there, or No, it's not there. Now, what can be leading in that with dealing with an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The manner in which you've framed the issue and framed the question is distinct from that which is being said by Ms. Edgerton. As you just said, he's being asked whether he can pick up the same here -- same theme here. Now, as a thematic approach, it's distinct from the question of "some evidence." It is that language that I am objecting to. If the question was framed as you had framed it, whether you pick up the same theme here, then I would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's check out what Madam Edgerton had asked. Now, the question was: "Dr. Donia, I apologise for all the preamble, but if you could look at this quotation of Mr. Krajisnik which begins with '... if we succeed with creating a federal BiH ...' and ends with '... the Serbian people should be united more than now than ever before ...' "Perhaps I should ask you this: Is this some evidence of continued support for the notion we have been discussing?" The answer to that would be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your position, and I stand by what I said. If she had asked the question with regard to a thematic response and do we have the same thematic issue, then I would not have stood on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The issue is whether or not this statement is consistent with the notion we've been discussing previously, Your Honours, and I think the issue comes across in the initial question. Either way, it's a yes or no answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then ask, Your Honour, that this 65 ter number - and, again, administratively, I'm going into -- I feel I'm going into murky waters, Your Honour - but 65 ter number 02079, pages 61 and 62 of the English and 78 and 79, be marked as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Including the page 1s?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They are so admitted. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They are exhibited as Exhibit P331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, perhaps I could ask you: Did this notion evolve in any way at all after the outbreak of war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This notion of -- you're referring, I take it, to the notion of a preference for Yugoslavia as federal Yugoslavia with the Serb state as the backup or secondary option?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because after -- or after the war began, the principal goal and activities of the Bosnian Serb leaders were directed at achieving international recognition for the Bosnian Serb polity. Therefore, the Yugoslav option was effectively dead, and the alternative became, then, the primary goal in the context of international recognition. So the precise form that this took now was to seek recognition for the Bosnian Serb polity, recognising in the practical sense that the road toward a unified state, unified Serb state, would become -- would be something down the road, sought to do nothing that would compromise the ultimate reaching that goal, but at the same time wanted to secure recognition as an important interim step on the way to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, at this juncture, I could ask for 65 ter number 2150.01 to be displayed, please. It's previously been marked - again, administrative murky waters, Your Honour - but it's been previously marked as Exhibit 218, but I'm not clear whether the whole document has been marked as Exhibit 218 or certain excerpted pages of the document. But I could certainly indicate which pages I would, in due course, be interested in displaying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit 218 is page 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could I ask for 02150.01, page 16 of the English transcript and, I think, page 16 of the Serbo-Croatian to be displayed, please. I see page 16, and there I note -- that's e-court page 16 of the English transcript. There I note Aleksa Buha is the speaker, and if we could just go slowly through his speech until we get to page 19. And, for the record and everyone's information, these are minutes of the 40th Assembly session, 40th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, held in Brcko on 11 May 1994. And in the English now, can we keep going slowly through until we come to e-court page 19, and then I'll deal with the location of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, just before we go ahead, can we just sort out how we name our exhibits. Exhibit 218 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- is 65 ter 02150.01. Now, you're using exactly the same 65 ter number here, and we are going to get a different exhibit number for this, but the 65 ter number is exactly the same. I think you've got to sort that one out first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, you'll have to sort out the 65 ter numbering here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do. If I may, Your Honour, just for clarity, and it will help certainly all of us in the future. Should the pages I'm refer to be accepted as exhibits, I would assume they would be marked as part of 02150.01. Am I correct in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, accepting that 0215.01 is already Exhibit 218.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And now this one is going to get a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we -- do we need to give it a different exhibit number if it's different pages of the same large document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will tell us what you want to do. If you want us to be part of that previous exhibit, then that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's what we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was talking across the aisle. I believe that's what we discussed. We actually had a meeting in which we were trying to figure out a way of coordinating this particular issue, when we're dealing with one exhibit and there are a number of different pages because it's a voluminous exhibit that are picked out. I believe that the solution suggested by Ms. Edgerton was what we discussed. We were going to try, as an experimental phase, to see whether or not it was going to work or not. But I believe what she's suggested is what had been discussed by all parties, including the register, and we also received the assistance of the Chamber. We were trying to figure out a way to make it work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I understood Madam Edgerton to be suggesting was that it be given a different exhibit number. Now, that won't work. If it comes under exactly the same 65 ter number, the only way is to then -- if this page 16 that she is now going to refer to is admitted into evidence, the only way, if it comes under that 65 ter number, is to make it part of Exhibit 218. That's the only way you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you agreed to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what we thought about doing, because that way you'd have -- you would have all in one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- package for that particular exhibit. That was the whole. There were some technical issues that we thought might be a problem, but we were getting research on those to see if they're going to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you go to page 19 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not 16 -- oh, you start at 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To identify who the speaker was, Your Honour, Mr. Aleksa Buha, and I'll ask a question about that in a few minutes. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, let me get the B/C/S on the screen and sorted first, please. Page 16 of the B/C/S transcript, second paragraph, starting at line 8 from the top of the paragraph, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if I could direct you to Mr. Buha's comments about two-thirds of the way down the paragraph on the right-hand side, beginning with the sentence, "As for ..." which appears on the far right-hand side of this paragraph, seven lines up from the bottom: "As for the political organisation ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you two questions. First of all, do you know who Aleksa Buha was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Aleksa Buha was -- he became the foreign minister of the Bosnian Serb polity -- of the Serbian -- of the Bosnian Serb polity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these articulations by Mr. Buha of the options available to the Bosnian Serb polity, do you view them as being consistent with your analysis of the evolution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This -- we see here this kind of new wrinkle in the post-war that began -- that was articulated after the war began already entering. That is, on the one hand, is the recognition of the Bosnian Serb polity internationally, and the other is ultimate unification with Serbia. Here he says, "... our primary option is still uniting with Serbia; and if not, then the alternative would be independence."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, could I ask that page 19 of the English translation of this 65 ter number 2150.01, and page 16 of the B/C/S be added to Prosecution Exhibit P218, please, as part of the exhibit, given that they're extracts from the same umbrella document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted, and they will become part of Exhibit P218.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we now move to 65 ter number 2226, please, a transcript of the 7th session of the Bosnian -- of the Assembly of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 15 February 1992. And on the B/C/S original, I'd like page 43, please, second paragraph from the bottom; on the English translation, I'd like, please, page 26, fourth paragraph. I hope that's correct, yes. Fourth paragraph, starting with "Let Serbia and Montenegro ..." Thank you. I see, perhaps for the sake of the record, we should go back to the previous page to identify the speaker -- Oh, no. Your indulgence, please. I apologise. Thank you. The speaker here is Mr. Vojo Kupresanin. That's on page 25, and if we could go over to page 26 again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, Dr. Donia, to the paragraph that begins, "As for the JNA ..." and the paragraph following that which begins, "Let Serbia and Montenegro ..." Can you see those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First of all, do you know who Mr. Kupresanin was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin was -- Kupresanin was at that time the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just explain in a nutshell, succinctly, what the Autonomous Region of the Krajina was for the benefit of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Krajina was the renamed Community of Municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, the organisation that was founded in late April 1991 in the Bosnian Krajina, consisting of Serb-majority municipalities in that area. In September of 1991, at the time that other Serbian autonomous regions were created, the Community of Municipalities of Bosnian Krajina was renamed to be closer in name to these other SAOs and was given the name ARK, or Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the articulations of Mr. Kupresanin that we've pointed to in these documents, do you view them as being consistent with your explanation of the evolution of this notion of the options available for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. At this time, he is again moving into it this -- towards this phase after the beginning of the war, when the prospect of Yugoslavia as a federal state has pretty well collapsed; and he's looking at, first of all, the Serbian republic, by which he means the Bosnian Serb polity, joining Serbia and Montenegro which are to be the nucleus of the future Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could these pages of 65 ter number 0226, and I would ask for the B/C/S pages 43 and 44, because I think the highlight quotations go over two pages, and page 26 of the English, be marked as exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, of course, page 1 also, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course. Madam Registrar, every time we admit an exhibit, we start with page 1 just to be able to see what the topics are about, and then the pages that are being admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will make a note in e-court. The document will become Exhibit P332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another 65 ter number, 2160.01, pages of which have previously been marked as P231, but not these pages, being transcripts of the 53rd session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, held in Jahorina on 28 August 1995. In the B/C/S, I'd like to take us to page 84, first paragraph. Tell me if I'm going too fast, please, Mr. Registrar. Page 84 -- no, I'm sorry, 84, not 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On my notes, Exhibit P231, I have it as 65 ter 01260, not 2160.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence, please, Your Honour, to let me check with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sometimes I transpose numbers, so I may be apologising to you very soon. We'll see. I'm informed by Ms. Javier that in e-court, 2160.01 is, indeed, P231. We should perhaps see if our records all correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe it's me who transposed numbers. Thank you. I'm sorry. I'll make the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Page 84, please, of the B/C/S, Mr. Registrar, first paragraph, ninth to the seventeenth line, to the best of what I'm informed; and the English translation, page 66. Your indulgence for a moment. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I always feel more comfortable if I can identify the sentence on the page with my own eyes before we proceed further, rather than just rattling out some instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like more time to do that, like a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That might be convenient, Your Honour. Thank you for the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton, you have now found your bearings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. If it please Your Honour, I'd just like to note for the record that the appearances have changed. Mr. Harmon has been called away, and I'm assisted now for the rest of today's session by my colleague Mr. Evangelos Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Welcome, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, my bearings have taken me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To page 66 of 65 ter 02160.01.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, beginning with the sentence approximately halfway down the page: "We have no desire to become a separate state," a statement by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see the remarks by Dr. Karadzic that I've just indicated for the record?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you please review that quotation right down to where we see, if I have it correctly, "... it's an attempt to secure both." Karadzic reads: "We have no desire to become a separate state," and further.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you view this statement as being consistent with your hypothesis, if I can call it that, about the evolving or the evolution of the options for the Bosnian Serb polity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This being in wartime, late in the war, we see that expression of a desire for ultimate unity with other Serb polities in the context of Yugoslavia, but also considering an interim step which would be recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, could this page 66 of the English language version and B/C/S page 84 be marked as additions to Exhibit P231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Donia, recognition by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This page is admitted into evidence and its corresponding B/C/S page, and they will form part of Exhibit P231. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, we've been dealing up until this point exclusively with expressions or articulations by the political leadership in the Republika Srpska and Serbia of the goals of the SDS. I'd like to know, have you seen in the course of your research evidence of RS military leaders expressing themselves on this same notion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are some expressions of this notion expressed within the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which was periodically addressed by senior generals of the Army of Republika Srpska, and also in interviews published in principally the Belgrade newspaper NIN.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What type of a newspaper was NIN? Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. NIN stands for Nedeljne Informativne Novine, which is a Weekly Informative Newspaper. It, as a weekly, did a lot of conventional stories, but also engaged in a lot of interviews with key players in the Yugoslav crisis throughout the 1990s. Some of those were quite extensive interviews. One case even went to devoting an entire issue to a series of interviews. So it was a remarkably independent newspaper operating in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask 65 ter number 1268 be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 1268?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1268. If we could go to e-court page 17, bottom right-hand corner on the B/C/S copy, thank you, and on the English version, pages 36 and 37, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just with respect to the first pages of these images, Dr. Donia, that you saw on the screen in front of you, did you recognise what they were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there was a picture of General Ratko Mladic on the cover of NIN.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could direct you to the second full paragraph on English page 36, it appears at the bottom of your screen so far: "That was the Operation Lukavac 93. What was the area it encompassed?" This is an interview with General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you scroll further down, please, Mr. Registrar, on the English page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the answer to that question that General Mladic gives, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar has just given you the last line of the answer to that question. Now, if we go back to the previous page in English, General Mladic refers to three names, Kupa, Korana, and Timok. Are you familiar with those names at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: All three are rivers. The Kupa is a small river that runs, in part, along the border between Croatia and Slovenia, and joins with the Korana river at Karlovac in Croatia. Timok is a river that for a very short period or short length defines the border between Serbia and Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, broadly speaking, then, when General Mladic refers to the aim of Operation Lukavac, Lukavac 93, as he does in this answer, as being, among other things, "the territorial unification of the Serbian people from Kupa and Korana to Timok" - and I'm quoting the article here - what geographic area does this encompass?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It would be a wide swathe of territory, including all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a good portion of Croatia, and all or most -- or at the very least, most of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you view this statement of General Mladic as consistent with the articulations we've been looking at so far of the notions of Serbian unity that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He suggests here that -- the "and" in that sentence suggests or states that the aim of the operation was joining parts of the Bosnian Serb polity, and, at the same, time contributing to the territorial unification of the Serb people over this much broader swathe of territory. Effectively, he is stating that the Bosnian Serb portion of this is a subset of the broader goal of Serb unification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder, Your Honours, if I could ask, then, that these pages of 65 ter 1268 - it's a 20-page article, Your Honour, in B/C/S; in English, substantially more - this B/C/S page 17 and English pages 36 and 37, plus page 1, be tendered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Edgerton. We'll do that in a moment. But, Mr. Donia, just so that you take me along - I may be slow on the uptake - this geographical area, he is describing an area where Operation Lukavac took place. Are you able to say whether this, in his mind, was what he would like or would have loved to see constituting an independent Serbian area, as he perceived it at the time; or did they just happen to be in those areas at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was part of what he would have loved to see and that part which was specifically the objective of Operation Lukavac 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And trying to follow you while you are talking and look at the map, I've been able to identify or to find on the map the rivers of Kupa and Korana. Where would Timok be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Timok is on the border with Bulgaria, far to the east, the border between Serbia and Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, sir. Those pages are then admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard to Serbian goals, Dr. Donia, I take from your two reports, you're familiar with the strategic objectives of 12 May 1992 --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Madam Interpreter. Could I have 65 ter number 02547 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you recognise the documents on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what are they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the excerpt from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska from November of 1993, in which the six strategic goals that were adopted on 12 May 1992 are published in what is probably their simplest and most authoritative form over the signature of -- or the printed signature of Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, are you aware of who announced these strategic objectives on 12 May 1992, prior to their adoption?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. They were introduced and outlined to the Bosnian Serb Assembly by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did these goals persist for the Bosnian Serb political and military leaders for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I've been able to identify many tens of references to these strategic objectives in the course of deliberations in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, always with the notion that they constitute the authoritative guidelines for action of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These strategic objectives, do you view them as being consistent with the political and military leaders' articulated notions of Serbian unity that we've been discussing here so far today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they are consistent. They are a somewhat more specific iteration of those goals pertaining to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Donia referred a little earlier to the fact that Serbian military leaders in Bosnia also did articulate this. He didn't mention the names of those leaders. I see you're still repeating the question and referring to political and military leaders articulating notions. Specifically which military leaders are these that you are referring to, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've mentioned General Mladic already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must have been asleep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I would also say General Gvero articulated those ideals in the course of his several addresses to the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. I probably didn't hear those references.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, can I ask Dr. Donia to explain who General Gvero is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, you're the dominus litus.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, who was -- when you speak of military leaders, you mentioned the name of General Gvero. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. General Gvero was the deputy commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army, the Army of Republika Srpska. He also served as the principal representative of the Main Staff to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, once General Mladic had withdrawn from attending the sessions in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just for completeness, who was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic was the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, at page 68, line 1, you noted that these objectives were consistent. You said "... a more specific iteration of those goals pertaining to Bosnia-Herzegovina," referring to the Bosnian Serb goals. I'd like to take you back to a couple of those goals by way of example. The second strategic objective refers to a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. To your mind, Dr. Donia, how is -- I'll ask you two questions. First of all, could you -- and I'll take you to a map in this regard. I'm going to ask you first, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, to identify the area covered by this corridor; and then, second, how it -- in what way that goal is consistent with the positions articulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. Because it takes some time to upload these images in e-court, Your Honour, I'd prefer to refer Dr. Donia to one of the maps in the map book, and put it on the ELMO so he can better illustrate his propositions to the Trial Chamber, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By his last answer, I think it might be more useful for him to refer to map 6 in the map book, and that's already been exhibited as P187.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could I now, looking at this map, just ask you to explain how the second strategic objective is consistent with the articulated goals.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for bringing me back to the world of paper and ELMO. The corridor in question runs between the large swathe of territory, many municipalities of which have a Bosnian Serb majority, to the west of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the area of Semberija, which is in the north-east corner of Semberija. The corridor as it existed through much of the conflict widened on both ends, but had a very limited width hugging the Sava River in the area from approximately Brcko to Bosanski Samac. Thus, the corridor really refers to this, let's say, area right here very close to the river, which was at times cut off by the forces of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian forces of the Croatian Defence Community. It was vital to the Serbs to have that open in order to keep the two large wings here of Bosnian-controlled -- Bosnian Serb-controlled territory contiguous with one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, I'm not sure whether you intend tendering the marked map, according to the witness's markings, at some stage; and if that's your intention, rather than use the pointer that he's using, maybe you would like him to use something that writes and he can mark it. That's, of course, if you want to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, looking at his explanation on the record, I think his explanation serves as a very good illustration of his proposition without tendering the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're the dominus litus.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we could move to the third objective, the establishment of the corridor in the Drina River Valley and the eradication of the Drina River as a border between the Serbian states.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you explain how, in your view, the achievement of this objective was consistent with this articulated notion of Serbian unity. You may be able to do this without the map. It's just by way of an illustrative tool.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, just for illustration, the Drina River originates here, flows north, and then comes to define the boundary between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia in this area, ultimately flowing into the Sava. That river has historically, that is, since about the nineteenth century, early nineteenth century, been -- frequently functioned as a border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serb strategic objectives wanted to eliminate that border so that it could be traversed more easily and enhance the unity between Serbia and the Serb-controlled areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You can remove that map from the ELMO now, and we'll revert back to e-court. I'd like to take us back, please, to the article from NIN, which has been marked as P133, the interview of Ratko Mladic, to page 37 of the e-court. The 65 ter was 1268. Oh, my apologies, 333. I'm grateful to all my colleagues for guiding me on this. Prosecution Exhibit 333. Now, page 37 of the English, thank you, and the B/C/S, page 17 again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, we earlier --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see the printing is a little bit difficult to read on the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's legible to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, not to me, with respect. Page 37 of the English version, I'd like to direct you to General Mladic's response in the way of the first two sentences to the very next question after the one we dealt with earlier. The question is: "The aim of the Operation Lukavac 93 was certainly to prevent the Drina from becoming the Serbian border, but at the same time Muslims had tried in every way to get to this river." Can you look at the first two sentences of General Mladic's response to this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we enlarge it a little bit. I know Madam Edgerton can now read it. I can't. It doesn't seem to work. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe if it assists, I can, with Your Honours' leave, I can read this out. It is a bit blurry still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, here General Mladic says: "For us Serbs west of the Drina, the River Drina had never been a border, nor will it ever be. The Drina is our backbone." Is this consistent -- is this articulation by General Mladic consistent with the strategic objective number 3 -- the realisation of strategic objective number 3?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It could almost -- it is very nearly a simple restatement of it in language that was probably more commonly used at the time among Bosnian Serb leaders, that "the Drina is our backbone."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we can move on please to 65 ter 06690, a transcript of the 20th RS Assembly session held on 14 and 15 September 1992. I'd like to direct us to the English, page 14, seventh line from the bottom of the page, a statement by Radovan Karadzic; and B/C/S page 16, fifteenth line from the bottom of the page. Mr. Registrar, is there any way you can enlarge the English a little bit further? That's not bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the fifteenth line up from the bottom of the page, Karadzic says - if I could have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour - at the sentence beginning "The Drina is of great strategic importance ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There we go. I see it halfway across. It's not the fifteenth line. It's the seventh line up from the bottom of the page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see the passage from Dr. Karadzic that I'm highlighting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is -- to your mind, is this statement by Karadzic an articulation of the importance of achieving strategic objective number 3 to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could please have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. I'm advised certain pages of this have already been entered as an objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies, Your Honour. This is Exhibit P203, and Ms. Javier's records indicate that the entire session has been exhibited. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go further to 65 ter 02305.01, which is a session of the Bosnian Serb -- sorry, the RS Assembly held in Bjelaca on the 3rd of April, 1993. If we could go in English, please, to page 38, the last paragraph on the page; and B/C/S page 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you, Dr. Donia, to a comment by an individual named Dusko Pejovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll try and get a legible version of the page up. That's not bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you to Mr. Pejovic where he refers to Gorazde as an oasis. I think it's about the ninth line from the top of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Let's see. Can you give me a sentence beginning?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's the sixth line up from the bottom: "It is an oasis that we have to clear up as soon as possible ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, Dr. Donia, are you familiar with who Dusko Pejovic is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, other than he was a member of the -- a delegate to the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a historian, Dr. Donia, are you familiar with events in the area under discussion in this passage, the area of Gorazde, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was the situation there at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa were three enclaves in Eastern Bosnia which at that time were surrounded by troops of the VRS, and were the subject of humanitarian aid being delivered, when possible, by -- under UNPROFOR escort. Gorazde, like the other two towns, were swelled with Bosnian Muslims who -- from other parts of Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina who'd been driven out or gathered in those towns for protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you, then, see Mr. Pejovic's statement as having any relation to the importance of strategic objective number 3 to the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In this statement, he adds the demographic dimension to the notion of establishing the Drina as a backbone or eliminating it as a border. He's stating here that the liberation of these territories must necessarily be a part of securing the region as they envision it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this 02305.01, B/C/S page 23, English page 38, be marked as an exhibit, please -- sorry, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour. I'm ahead of myself. My apologies. We're on 65 ter 6690. I misquoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are on 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were right. Now you are wrong. We are on 65 ter 03205.01, page 38 in the English. It is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P335, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your patience, Your Honour, and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We shall stay patient, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. 65 ter 2143.01 is the next document, I'd like to direct us to; and that should be the transcript of the 33rd session of the Republika Srpska Assembly held in Mrkonjic Grad on 21 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please just repeat the 65 ter number. It's not appearing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, an administrative note, for some reason, since we resumed, these documents, the definition on them electronically, all seems to be rather fuzzy, and it's not making things easy for any of us, I suspect. I thought it might have been the scanning of the first document, but we seem to be seeing this phenomenon as we go through the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, ma'am. Is the origin of this phenomenon in the OTP? Quiet. Quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It may be my eyes, Your Honour. My colleague is informing me that I'm the only one this time that has a blurry transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not the only one. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since we're taking a moment and dealing with administrative matters, I have been informed that with regard to P203, the entire document was not admitted; rather, pages 1 and, I believe, 55 were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pages 1 and 55?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood. I think, at some point, we better double-check it to make sure, because I think that may be a document in its entirety which has not been admitted. I don't know if you want to take the time to deal with that right now or at the conclusion of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with it right now, if we can double-check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me say, my notes don't indicate that any specific pages were admitted, but they also indicate that this was marked for identification, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. My notes indicate that pages 1 and 55 were the pages that were in discussion, and, I believe, yes, marked for identification. It's also a document, I believe, that's under seal. Oh, wait a minute. I take that back. I take that back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Are we able to get guidance either from the Registry or from the case manager?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If this might be of some help - it may be, I don't know, because I don't know if I'm assisting - P217, the entire document was admitted and they both deal with 20th sessions. They're two different 20th sessions, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Accepting that, P217 is a different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. I'm just trying to figure out why we're having the decolage that we're having right now. I can't figure that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And according to my notes, Exhibit P217 was not admitted in its entirety. It was pages 6, 12, and 13 that were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. Then that became -- I'm sorry. I'm making it more confusing as opposed to less, because that became D8 because we admitted the entire document. Never mind, forget about what I just said. I was trying to make it easier. What I think I am doing is making it more difficult. Going back to the original situation that we're in, forgetting about P217, my notes do not reflect the entire document was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're now talking about P203.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. I'm just going back to that. I thought I could be of some help, but apparently I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I guess the Registry will take precedence. According to the Registry, the entire document was admitted, so we'll defer to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In which case, if the entire document was admitted, then where we are today at 65 ter 06690, page 14, will become part of Exhibit P203. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask the parties to double-check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry for trying to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your help is always appreciated, sir. But we can double-check that during the break and see whether everybody's correct. We're now back at 65 ter 02143.01.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please. If we could go to page 54 on the English, first paragraph, second and third line -- no. I'm sorry, Your Honours. That's not what I have marked here, but I'd like to -- yeah, that's what I have marked here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you, Dr. Donia, to the first paragraph, second and third lines, where you see Dr. Karadzic's -- an extract from a statement by Dr. Karadzic as to the significance of the Drina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have the B/C/S up?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, you can. With respect, I need to get one at a time before I see them. The B/C/S is page 34, second paragraph from the bottom of the page, last three lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the meanwhile, Dr. Donia, did you have a chance to look at the excerpt I've highlighted from -- a statement by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. What have you highlighted, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The sentence that begins "The significance of the Drina for Republika Srpska ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the passage ends with "... at this Assembly," the passage of interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you find this statement also consistent with what we've been discussing as being the importance of achieving the third strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this could be marked as an exhibit, please. 65 ter number, as I've indicated, is 2143.01. We're on page 34, and the corresponding B/C/S is page 54 -- Sorry, Your Honours. I think it's probably my fatigue, but again, I've inverted the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's page 54 in the English, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you to Ms. Javier for guiding me, as she does so ably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, over the course of your research, have you come to a view as to how you would characterise the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, I think they were carefully considered, adopted unanimously by the Assembly, and were guidelines which were considered firm guidelines for the civilian and military objectives of the Bosnian Serbs in the course of the war and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, from what you're saying, are we to understand that you would characterise these strategic objectives of 12 May 1992 as both political and military goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. They were determined by political leaders, passed on to military commanders, who then accepted them as goals for their own operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In relation to this, I'd like to take you to a document you've referred to in your background report on the Sarajevo siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 2070.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see this document on the screen in front of you, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These are minutes of a meeting held on May 14, 1992, attended by several major military leaders and presidents of a number of Serbian municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you speak of important military leaders, perhaps I could draw your attention to the first name mentioned on the list of attendees at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's on page 1 of the English, note 1; and page 1 of the B/C/S also, note 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who's the first name on the list of attendees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Colonel Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this individual?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He at this time was commander of the 30th Partisan Division, which was operating in or based in Bosnian Krajina. He subsequently went on to become a general and commander of the Romanija units of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this document, could you explain to us -- or do you attach any significance to this document in terms of the theme that we've moved on to, the strategic objectives as political and military goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. It is, first of all, an indication of the need that was felt for close coordination between civilian leaders and military commanders in the areas of operation of the military and the individual municipalities. It, furthermore, highlights the strategic goals or objectives that were presented two days before in the Assembly -- Bosnian Serb Assembly session in Banja Luka, and repeated or -- repeated with similar but not quite identical language by participants in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, going back to page 83, line 16 to 19, you mentioned that Galic became the commander of the Romanija units of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska. Are you aware what generally the activities of the Romanija units of the VRS were during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Those were units responsible for the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we can, in this document, go over to page 2 of the English, thank you, just to give Dr. Donia an opportunity to have a view of the document in its entirety, page 3 and page 4. The next page on the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, looking at the points listed at the top of page 4, numbers 2 to 6, could I draw your attention to item number 5 which says: "It was stated that Sarajevo must either be divided or razed to the ground."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you attach any significance to this; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it indicates that not everyone walked away from the session on the 12th of May with the notion that Sarajevo should only be divided, and, as such, represents his belief that the notion advanced was that Sarajevo should either by divided or razed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This being who? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I missed the speaker here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the earlier page, please, the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the president of Mrkonjic Grad municipal assembly, Mr. Malidza, who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be tendered adds an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to go to a further document which has actually already been admitted as an exhibit, P149; 65 ter number 00379. If we can -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see the documents on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: These are, in English and the original B/C/S, the report prepared in the course of 199 -- early 1993, I believe, on the status and combat-readiness of the VRS in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I take all of us to page 159 of the translation and the B/C/S page 43, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could I direct you to, I think, the fourth line in this first full paragraph that begins with the phrase, "The strategic objectives of our war," and ask you to review that passage down to the end of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could scroll down slowly, it may take the rest of us some time to have a look as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at the passage I've identified, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, generally speaking, is this passage consistent with your articulated view that the strategic objectives were not only political but military objectives as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. They would be consistent with my view that they were -- they originated with the civilian leadership and were assigned to and accepted by the military leaders of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of this document, I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Apparently, the B/C/S version is too small for Mr. Perisic to be able to read it in the original, so I don't know if it can be enlarged or if Ms. Edgerton could just read out what she's referring to, then he would be appreciative of what specifically is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is it possible to enlarge it? Mr. Perisic, are you able to see it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently, it's the wrong page. I'm going to defer here to Mr. Lukic because he's a native speaker and he might be of a little bit more assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This page in the B/C/S version, although it has these dots and visually seems to correspond to the English version, has absolutely nothing to do with the English version. These things are totally different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, can you come to the rescue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, it would be simplest if Ms. Edgerton just read the text out in English, and then we'll be able to hear what the interpreters from the B/C/S booth have to say. This will make it easier for us to follow, because otherwise it will be difficult for us to follow everything. If it is read out in English and interpreted into B/C/S, the witness can then give his opinion, and it will be easier for all of us to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, I am, Your Honours, and I wouldn't be able to provide you with any other kind of hard copy or answer as quickly as it would take me to read the relevant portion out, so with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Just put the copy of the translation on, read it, and let it be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Registrar, with respect, I can't read the Cyrillic version. Page 159 of the translation, please. I see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now been provided with the page in the B/C/S version, and it corresponds to the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just wait for the registrar to give us the English side of the story.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Your Honours, if I may, I would like to make a correction regarding Exhibit P203 which he discussed earlier. Only pages 1, 51, and 55 were admitted on 10 November; therefore, page 14 is admitted today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Madam Registrar, and I think that's what we did today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, not to leave P149 immediately, just for the sake of absolute clarity, and for the record, which is, of course, most important, can I indicate that this page, which Mr. Lukic says is the corresponding page, bears the ERN number 0060-7477. And if I could have some guidance as to which e-court page number this is, that would be very helpful, because on my screen it only shows up as page 1 of 1, or a 65 ter number; just to make sure we have all the information to be able to identify this page on the record. I'm advised it's page 139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 139 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, I'm advised it's page 139 of 65 ter 00379. Perhaps, since this matter is going to go over until tomorrow, Mr. Lukic and I could just double-check that, and advise Your Honours tomorrow morning as to what we're able to agree on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should say, Your Honour, I'm about to move into another theme, and I note the time. I'm in Your Honours' hands. It's not going to be a five-minute theme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got ten. I don't whether you can -- can it be a ten-minute theme?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll see, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, to remain with your report on the background to the siege of Sarajevo, I'd like to refer to page 3 of that report where you noted reference to the census of 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You're familiar with that census?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I've been looking at it for a number of years with the purpose of understanding the situation on the eve of the war and also the changes in demographic distribution of groups from earlier censuses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this and earlier censuses you've mentioned, are these the only sources you've consulted with a view to understanding the changes of -- changes in demographic distribution of groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. The whole issue of the 1991 census was, in fact, then and remains, controversial, so there is a substantial body of literature in the press from the time and subsequent articles analysing the census and assessing its validity and its import.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of exactly what other sources you've consulted in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there are some articles by demographers. There are some articles - I can't give you specific names - but there's a very nice article by a human demographer -- I'm sorry, a geographer, human geographer, in a journal that looks at the relationship between the competition between groups and subsequent violence in individual municipalities. There was also a very, I thought, illuminating series of articles in Oslobodjenje at the time about the census and its significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Given all this, I wonder if you could very briefly explain to us how the different ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina were distributed around the republic -- former republic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There was a broad distribution throughout the republic of -- throughout most of the republic of all three major ethnic groups. The distribution had some exceptions. There are very few -- or were very few Croats along the eastern part of Bosnia. There is a swathe of territory in western Herzegovina which is, for all practical purposes, purely Croat; another part of the western segment of Bosnia that is almost exclusively Serb; and, finally, kind of an enclave in the north-west which is almost exclusively Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if I could now call up a map which appears as 65 ter number 9224. It's map 5 in Your Honours' map books, Your Honours' and my friends' map books. That might take a couple of minutes to come up. 9224. Very quick.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see a map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map produced by a private provider AlterMedia on the basis of census results from 1991 which presents the distribution of ethnic groups by municipalities in a rather unusual way. It gives -- it assigns a colour to the majority group in that municipality, whether that majority is absolute or relative; and then represents other groups by means of vertical bars. And in a series of data that I think are very difficult to accurately present visually, this comes as close as I have seen of representing the situation in each individual municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to be -- so that we're all clear, is each ethnic group assigned a different colour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I see this map is in various shades of green, red, and blue. Can you explain what those colours represent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The red is Serbs. The red colour is Serb absolute majority in that municipality; lined-through is Serb relative majority. Blue is Croats, and green is Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you worked with and analysed this map before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you compared the data as represented in this map to other demographic sources you've consulted in the course of your research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you find the representations, then, on this map to be reliable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, going back again to the strategic objectives that we've discussed earlier and where you referred to another map as an illustrative tool, could I now ask you to take the computer pen from the monitor in front of you and indicate the territorial parameters, approximately, of strategic objective number 2; that being a corridor between Semberija and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. This is fancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome to the world of technology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That corridor runs just approximately - and I'd have to say it's at most an approximation - but the bar of the barbell here is what we're speaking to in the case of the -- what's called the corridor or the Posavina Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated, on the record, you've drawn a barbell, so I see that, two circles linked by an oblong. Could you explain what the circle on the right-hand represents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, that's Semberija area with its probably major city being Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the bar on -- sorry, the circle on the left-hand?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The circle on the left is my rather pathetic representation of the territory of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the oblong between the two?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the area of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your view, and looking at what you've mapped out on this map, does the achievement or would the achievement of strategic objective number 2 transect any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The achievement of the strategic goal would transect a large population of Croats and Muslims in the Posavina Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, again, using this map as an illustration, could you roughly indicate the territorial parameters of strategic objective 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I wonder if there's a way, Mr. Registrar, that Dr. Donia could do that in another colour than the red colour that he's marked with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think you can go ahead, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Recognising that the goal itself was imprecise and my representation will be even less precise, we're talking approximately about this area there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the area that you've marked in blue representing, very approximately as you've indicated, the territory covered by strategic objective number 3, in your view and using this map as an illustration, would the achievement of strategic objective number 3 transect any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. As I've indicated, there are very few Croats living in -- were very few Croats living in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the eastern boundary, but it transects an area which is very mixed population -- has a very mixed population of Bosnian Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, if you can work towards rounding up your ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can round it very quickly, Your Honour, if I could request that this be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're ending there with your strategic objectives --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The map as marked is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Noting the time, Your Honour, perhaps it would be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Donia, we are still not done with you. I'm sure I'm carrying coal to Newcastle when I say to you, while you're in the witness stand, you may not discuss this case with anybody else - not with your counsel, not with anybody - until you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we stand adjourned until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
